newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Civil Guard out of sorts, out of cash.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Civil Guard out of sorts, out of cash.

text.p: Spain's Civil Guard chief has disclosed that the paramilitary force is in disarray and short of millions of dollars after 13 years of Socialist government, a guard spokesman said on Wednesday.

The new Popular Party government said it had inherited a 41 billion peseta ($323 million) Civil Guard budget shortfall made up of back pay, fuel and telephone bills and construction debts which still left only half the 2,423 barracks in good repair.

"It's true, there was a budget hole of 41 billion pesetas," the spokesman said, confirming details of a budget report that Civil Guard chief Santiago Lopez Valdivielso presented to a parliamentary committee on Tuesday.

The Civil Guard, which is responsible for policing rural areas and highways and takes a leading role in anti-terrorist activities, was found to have built luxury barracks with heated swimming pools, while leaving others in disrepair.
Valdivielso used the opportunity to publicly criticise his predecessor, Luis Roldan, saying it was criminal to build such barracks while others were in ruins.

"There had been poor use of resources during the Socialist era that left tremendous disarray in the (force)," Valdivielso said in the report. "It seems others were more worried about more lucrative affairs."
The Guard has historically been both respected for helping motorists in need and reviled as symbols of repression under the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco.

Roldan, who was the first civilian head of the 70,000 strong force in its 150-year history, is currently on trial for embezzlement and corruption charges related to illegal Civil Guard contracts and activities.

He scandalised the current conservative administration when he accused now Defence Minister Eduardo Serra of paying $1 million in bribes for Civil Guard construction contracts when Serra was a top executive at major construction firm Cubiertas.

Roldan had already blackened the Civil Guard's reputation and embarrassed the Socialist government when he was first accused of wrongdoing and fled the country in 1994. He was on the run for months before being tracked down in Laos.

The Civil Guard's name was further damaged by allegations that some members were part of a "dirty war" campaign against ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) activists that killed 27 people, one third of them by mistake, from 1983 to 1987.
A highly-decorated Civil Guard general, who led the fight against guerrillas in the Basque country, is facing charges that he used torture, kidnap and murder against ETA separatists.
Former Socialist officials responsible for the Civil Guard, including ex-interior minister Jose Barrionuevo, have also been indicted on dirty war charges.

Valdivielso said he didn't know how he would recover the financial debt, but said he would work to repair the tattered Civil Guard reputation by operating strictly within the law and with respect for human rights.

"We are aware that some sectors of society believe there don't have to be limits and the end justifies the means," Valdivielso said. "But this is a mistake. Only a strict respect for legality makes us different from the terrorists."
